modes.name: Fabrication
modes.summary: Code that calls functions, methods or packages that don't exist.
setup: 348 fabricated completions (fake imports, fake methods, undefined names), written by Claude Sonnet 4.5 and verified to fail; 288 clean originals of the same code.
Static tools see the whole file with its 99 packages installed. AI tools see a diff with 15 lines of context.
Static tools count only findings that a symbol doesn't exist. A flag on a clean original is a false positive.

Temperature 0 (gpt-6-luna: its default, no temperature sent), one run each. Models on Hyperbolic, except gpt-6-luna, grok-4.1-fast and Phi-4-mini on Azure AI Foundry, and gpt-oss-20b and Qwen3.8-27B self-hosted with vLLM on one RTX 4090. Run 2026-11-19.
caveats: The fakes were made on purpose and the dataset picked hard cases; real agent mistakes may be easier or harder.
Static tools and AI tools saw different inputs and are scored at different granularity (line vs change).
Models asked directly were told exactly what to look for: an upper bound, not a product.

modes.summary: The agent edits, weakens or skips tests so failures disappear instead of fixing the code.
setup: 56 agent sessions labeled Test Modification (TRACE 1.1.1) vs 249 clean sessions. 212 sessions with other kinds of cheating are reported apart, not scored.
Every tool reads the full session transcript: messages, tool calls and tool output (median about 41,000 characters).

modes.name: Security vulnerability
modes.dataset: SusVibes (LeiLiLab, MIT): AI agents' patches for 166 real feature tasks, with hidden CVE tests
modes.summary: The agent's code change introduces a security vulnerability.
setup: 1243 vulnerable vs 459 secure patches, written by 26 agent runs (Claude, Gemini, GLM, Kimi, Qwen with SWE-agent, OpenHands, CLIs). Both kinds pass the task's functional tests; vulnerable ones fail the hidden CVE security test. Identical patches kept once; patches over 60k characters left out.

AI tools see the task text and the agent's diff. bandit and semgrep run on the patched files and flag a patch when a finding lands on a line it added. giskard and promptfoo wrap the same review in their own judge template, with deepseek-v4-flash as the judge.
Same review prompt for every model; temperature 0 (gpt-6-luna: its default). Answers cut off by the token limit are re-run at 32k. Run 2026-11-19/20.

Also tried on a 417-patch held-out subset (projects kept apart): claude-opus-4-8 at low effort J -2.8% (flags almost nothing), Kimi-K2.6 +6.1%, Muse Glimmer 30B +5.0% before and -1.7% after fine-tuning on the other 682 patches.
caveats: Every tool scores close to chance: telling these vulnerable patches from secure ones by reading the change is beyond them.
Check of the setup: with the vulnerable and the fixed version of the same code side by side (the CVE fix reverted), the best models reach only J +10 to +15%. So the low scores are not a scoring bug.

Label check: Opus (medium effort), shown the CWE, the real CVE fix and the security test, agreed with 78% of a sample of 'vulnerable' labels and 80% of 'secure' ones. About 20% label noise each way shrinks every J by about 40%.
Without such hints even Opus at medium effort tells apart only 6 of 50 vulnerable/fixed versions of the same code (J +10%): these flaws are mostly missing checks that don't show in a diff.
Dropping tasks with over-strict security tests (exact error-message checks, or no agent ever passing) raises J by only 1–5 points.
Unreadable answers (no verdict) count as not flagged: ultramarine 383, promptfoo 322, deepseek-v4.1 169 of 1,702.
51 patches could not be rebuilt as files (binary or missing vendored files); the static tools count them as not flagged.

modes.name: Logic error
modes.dataset: Collu-Bench (lt-asset, BSD-3-Clause-Clear): MBPP and HumanEval functions written by 11 code models
modes.summary: The code runs but computes the wrong result.
setup: 1536 functions that run but fail a test assertion vs 904 correct solutions, across 379 tasks. Code by 11 models (CodeLlama, DeepSeek-Coder, StarCoder2, Llama 3, gpt-4o-mini).
Every label re-checked by running the code against its tests: crashes, timeouts, 'wrong' outputs that actually pass and reference solutions that fail were dropped.
Reviewers see the task description and the function, not the tests. Same prompt for every model; temperature 0 (gpt-6-luna: its default). Run 2026-11-20.
caveats: Short, self-contained functions from two famous public problem sets: models may know the right answers, so these scores are an upper bound for real agent code.
The correct functions are reference solutions, the wrong ones model-written: style differs between the two classes.
Type checkers and linters look for a different kind of bug; they are here as a floor, not as fair competitors.

KG tools run through their own built-in check, with deepseek-v4-flash as their model: uqlm re-solves the task 5 times and flags code that disagrees with most re-solves; it was run on the first 300 + 300 functions only (it makes 10 model calls per review), and 62 of its answers were unreadable (counted as not flagged).

modes.name: Incomplete execution
modes.dataset: SWE-rebench-OpenHands-Trajectories (Nebius, CC-BY-4.0): Qwen3-Coder-480B in OpenHands on real GitHub issues
modes.summary: The agent declares the task done, but the work does not actually resolve it.
setup: 600 runs where the agent finished and declared the task done but the issue's hidden tests fail, vs 600 where it declared done and the tests pass. One run per issue; an issue is never on both sides.
Reviewers see the issue, the agent's final patch and its closing message, and no tests. Same prompt for every model; temperature 0 (gpt-6-luna: its default). Run 2026-11-20.
caveats: 'Not done' here means the hidden tests fail: that includes wrong fixes as well as unfinished ones, so this mode overlaps with logic error.

The KG's stub signal (TODO, pass, NotImplementedError in the diff) does not define the label: across 60,739 finished runs, stub markers appear about as often in passing runs (2,092) as in failing ones (2,208).
All runs come from one agent (Qwen3-Coder-480B with OpenHands).

Unreadable answers count as not flagged: deepseek-v4-flash 369 of 1,200 (mostly thinking past 32k tokens without answering), mimo 120, Phi 23. (Re-scored 2026-11-20 after a parser fix recovered 10 answers whose JSON was incomplete.) Phi almost never calls a run incomplete.

The KG's task-completion judges (Phoenix, Opik, DeepEval; each through its own built-in check, with deepseek-v4-flash as its model) almost never call a finished run incomplete (they flag 2-13% of failing runs): given the agent's own 'done' message, they believe it. PR-Agent's review flags about a third of failing runs but a quarter of passing ones too. Opik and PR-Agent were run on the first 150 + 150 runs only (PR-Agent takes about 4 minutes per review). Not runnable on a finished patch: PR-Agent ticket compliance (needs a linked GitHub or Jira ticket), TruLens Plan Adherence and DeepEval Step Efficiency (need the agent's step traces).

modes.name: Scope creep
modes.pos_label: patches with an injected unrequested change
modes.dataset: Synthetic, built on SWE-rebench-OpenHands-Trajectories (Nebius, CC-BY-4.0): correct agent patches + one change injected by Claude Opus
modes.summary: The agent makes changes nobody asked for while solving the task.
setup: 175 correct agent patches (Qwen3-Coder-480B in OpenHands, hidden tests pass) with ONE unrequested change injected by claude-opus-4-8, vs 175 correct patches from other issues left as they are.

Injected changes, 2-15 lines, in five kinds: drive-by refactor, cleanup, extra feature, quiet behaviour change, added logging/config. 127 sit in a file the agent already edited, 48 in another file of the same package. Each was checked to still parse; a sample was checked by hand.

Both sides use only near-minimal patches (no bigger than the reference fix allows) and are matched exactly on how many source files they change (23 injected patches without an exact match were dropped), so neither size nor file count gives the label away.

Reviewers see the issue and the patch. Same prompt for every model; temperature 0 (gpt-6-luna: its default). Run 2026-11-20. Building the set cost $13 of Opus calls, failed attempts included (not part of any tool's cost).
caveats: Synthetic: the unrequested changes were written by a model on purpose. Natural scope creep may be subtler or messier.
The 'clean' side was filtered to near-minimal patches, but some may still hold small unrequested edits; that would inflate FPR.
All patches come from one agent (Qwen3-Coder-480B with OpenHands).
None of the KG's scope-creep tools can be run on a finished patch: 20 of 22 prevent it during the run (approval gates, allow-lists, sandboxes); the other 2 are configurable LLM judges.

modes.name: Obsolescence
modes.dataset: Wang et al. (ICSE'25) deprecated-API map (65 pairs, 8 libraries) + solutions written by 5 models, deprecated call swapped in
modes.summary: The code uses a deprecated or removed library API.
setup: 155 solutions with the modern API swapped back to its deprecated twin vs 155 untouched solutions, all written by the same 5 models (gpt-6-luna, grok-4.1-fast, Phi-4-mini, deepseek-v4-flash, mimo) for the same tasks, across numpy, pandas, scipy, scikit-learn, seaborn, PyTorch, TensorFlow and transformers.

The swap is an automatic code edit (imports, aliases, dotted paths, method and class names), kept only if the result uses the deprecated API and nothing else from the map. Run with the latest libraries, 77 swapped solutions fail on load (ImportError, DeprecationWarning, ...) and 129 of 131 untouched ones run clean (TensorFlow not checked).

Plus 4 hand-written pairs for LLM SDKs. Anthropic: a call that names Claude 3.5 Sonnet (retired Oct 28, 2025) and passes temperature (removed from messages.create in SDK 1.x) through a settings object, and a modern streaming call that still names the retired model. Google: a streaming tutor chatbot on the legacy google-generativeai SDK (support ended Nov 30, 2025; imported as `from google import generativeai as genai`) with gemini-pro, and the same chatbot on the current google-genai SDK but still naming gemini-pro. Clean twins use claude-sonnet-5-5 / gemini-3.8-flash on the current SDKs.
Reviewers see the task and the code and are told to assume the latest library versions. Same prompt for every model; temperature 0 (gpt-6-luna: its default). Run 2026-11-20.
caveats: The LLM-SDK pairs are the hard ones: only the legacy Google SDK was caught (gpt-6-luna and mimo, and pyright with the current google-genai installed). Nobody caught a retired model ID inside otherwise current code (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, gemini-pro), nor temperature hidden in a settings object; grok flagged all eight samples, clean twins included. Retirements newer than a model's training need current documentation.
Synthetic: the deprecated calls were swapped in; models writing freely today rarely use these APIs (49 of 956 solutions).
53 positives use APIs that are deprecated but still present (mostly PyTorch); on removed APIs only, J is about the same for the top three.

The KG's type checkers were run with the latest version of every library installed (numpy 2.5, pandas 3.1, scipy 1.18, scikit-learn 1.9, PyTorch 2.15, transformers 5.23, current Anthropic and Google SDKs): they catch removed APIs (missing attribute or import) and APIs marked @deprecated, so pyright beats most models for free; mypy finds far fewer because many libraries ship no type information for it. They cannot see a retired model name. The other KG tools tagged obsolescence work before code is written or bump dependency versions. The two ruff rule sets are outside baselines and cover only NumPy 2 and Python-syntax upgrades.

modes.name: Supply chain
modes.dataset: Synthetic, hand-designed on SWE-rebench-OpenHands-Trajectories (Nebius, CC-BY-4.0) + OpenSSF malicious-packages names
modes.summary: The agent adds a dependency that is a malicious lookalike of a real package.
setup: 148 pairs of correct agent patches where the agent also adds 2-3 dependencies to the repo's own manifest (requirements files, setup.py, setup.cfg, pyproject, tox.ini). The two patches of a pair are identical except one dependency line: in one it is a known-malicious PyPI package (each has an OpenSSF/OSV record), in the other a genuine package.

Malicious names: 82 subtle typos of popular packages (plural, doubled/dropped/swapped letter, keyboard slip, digit, py- prefix; e.g. coloramas, urllib33) and 66 'popular name + word' combosquats (e.g. httpx-utils, twilio-rest).

Genuine names, all checked on PyPI (3+ releases, first release before Nov 2024, mature version): 53 real plugin-style packages (e.g. dask-awkward, pytest-enabler), 44 real packages one letter away from a famous one (e.g. pep257, pyqrcode), 51 obscure real packages from the repos' environments. 66 of 148 are outside PyPI's top 15,000, so popularity alone does not vouch for them.

The other added dependencies are packages actually installed in that repo's environment, at their real versions. Reviewers see the issue and the patch. Same prompt for every model; temperature 0 (gpt-6-luna: its default). Run 2026-11-20. The cases were designed by Claude (the coding assistant building this benchmark), not generated by any reviewed model.
caveats: The typosquat rule wins because it knows PyPI download ranks: on pairs whose genuine package is popular (top 15,000) it scores J +99%, on pairs whose genuine package is obscure only +65%. The best model (gpt-6-luna) is steadier: +73% and +82%.
Models' false alarms come mostly from genuine lookalikes (real packages one letter from a famous one): gpt-6-luna flags 36% of them, mimo 57%. Phi-4-mini never flagged anything.
Synthetic: real agents add a malicious dependency rarely; this tests whether a reviewer notices one, not how often agents do it.

Only known-malicious names: a lookup in OSV/OpenSSF would catch every one of them, and none of them can be installed from PyPI today (all removed). The test is what a reviewer reading the diff can tell.
Most KG supply-chain tools (Socket, Snyk, Dependabot, Renovate) need accounts or GitHub and were not run; the two rules are simple stand-ins for name-reputation checks.
2 pairs (4 patches) were blocked by Hyperbolic's firewall for deepseek and mimo on every try; like other unreadable answers they count as not flagged.

modes.name: Dependency blindness
modes.pos_label: patches that re-implement something already available
modes.dataset: Hand-built on SWE-rebench-OpenHands-Trajectories (Nebius, CC-BY-4.0): correct agent patches, one call re-implemented by hand
modes.summary: The agent writes its own version of something the codebase, the standard library or an installed package already provides.
setup: 50 pairs. Each starts from one correct agent patch (Qwen3-Coder-480B in OpenHands, hidden tests pass) that uses an existing function. In the positive, that use is replaced by a hand-written re-implementation; the two patches of a pair are identical everywhere else.

What is re-implemented: 30 of the repository's own helpers (e.g. PyJWT's base64url decoding, MONAI's ensure_tuple, oauthlib's raise_from_error, MetPy's check_units decorator), 17 standard-library functions (e.g. shlex.split, fnmatch, os.makedirs(exist_ok=True), csv.writer, functools.wraps, uuid4) and 3 NumPy functions (np.where, np.isclose, np.setdiff1d). How: 33 inline (the call replaced by a few lines), 11 rewritten helpers, 6 copies of the helper's body pasted into the patch.

Each edit was checked: the file still parses, no undefined name is added (ruff F821), the original call is gone and the re-implementation is there. Seven hand-rolled helpers were extracted from the positive patches and run against the function they replace; they agree on the kind of input the patch passes (e.g. shlex.split 6 of 6, fnmatch 36 of 36, fountain's stringify 7 of 8: -0.0 differs). Others differ on edge cases, as hand-rolled code does (time-zone-aware indexes, error classes).

Reviewers see the issue, the patch and, when the re-implemented function is the repository's own, the module that defines it (both patches of a pair see the same files). Same prompt for every model; temperature 0 (gpt-6-luna: its default). Run 2026-11-20. The pairs were written by Claude (the coding assistant building this benchmark), not by any reviewed model.
caveats: Hand-built: every re-implementation was written on purpose. Natural dependency blindness is often larger (whole helpers rebuilt) or subtler.

The clean side can already be blind: 8 of 58 drafted pairs were dropped because the agent's own patch already re-implemented something (e.g. sorting version tags as strings although pre_commit.util.parse_version exists). Found by reading every base patch and by checking every clean patch the strong models flagged. Some may remain, which would inflate FPR.
Showing the module that defines the helper makes the task easier than real review, where the reviewer must know or find it; read the scores as an upper bound.

sentrux, the KG's redundancy checker, was not run: its macOS release binary needs a Gatekeeper quarantine override to start, which was not approved for this run. The rule here is a simple stand-in for its documented duplicate-body check and only catches copied bodies.
Unreadable answers count as not flagged: Phi-4-mini 18 of 100 (15 Azure connection failures after retries, 3 malformed), deepseek-v4-flash 1.
50 pairs: confidence intervals are about +/-10 points.

findings: A cheap model asked directly is the best reviewer in 8 of 9 modes.
The exception is Supply chain, where a typosquat rule wins.
The three strongest cheap models are close: within 10 points of each other in 8 of 9 modes.
Average J: gpt-6-luna +68%, deepseek-v4-flash +67%, mimo-v2.6-flash +68%. None costs more than $3.80 per 1,000 reviews in any mode.
Two modes nobody handles yet: Security vulnerability (best J +8%) and Incomplete execution (best J +19%).
No model, program or judge we ran reaches J 25% there.
Free programs pay off where the failure is a checkable fact: pyright on Fabrication (+85%); pyright (latest libraries) on Obsolescence (+57%); a typosquat rule on Supply chain (+84%).
The best free option scores J under 15% on Security vulnerability, Logic error, Incomplete execution, Scope creep, Dependency blindness.
Wrapping the model in a review tool did not help: PR-Agent runs on deepseek-v4-flash, yet scores below deepseek-v4-flash asked directly in 4 of 4 modes.
Fabrication +69% vs +92%; Security vulnerability -1% vs +5%; Logic error +28% vs +69%; Incomplete execution +7% vs +17%.
Small and non-reasoning models fall short: Phi-4-mini scores J under 20% in 7 of 8 modes,
and grok-4.1-fast (no reasoning) flags 47% of clean samples on average, against 16% for the three models above.
caveats: J compares tools within a mode. Across modes it only roughly reflects difficulty: each dataset was built differently (real agent runs, execution-checked model code, synthetic injections, hand-built pairs), so a high J on a hand-built synthetic mode is not as hard-won as a low one on real agent runs.
Averages weight every mode equally and cover only the modes a tool ran (the number is in brackets).
mypy, ruff and the simple rules show the best configuration we ran in each mode; hover a cell to see which. pyright and mypy on Obsolescence ran with the latest libraries installed.
Same prompt style for every model, temperature 0 (gpt-6-luna: its default), one run each; no tool was tuned per mode. Findings above are computed from the table, so they update with it.

star_modes.name: Cascading failure
star_modes.description: The agent detects an error and attempts a fix that introduces NEW errors; repeated iterations spiral further from the working state.
star_modes.note: No dedicated tool yet. The KG's only tag is borderline: agent-governance-toolkit's circuit breakers stop error-rate runaways, not fix-spirals, and it is an experimental template.

tools.name: agent-governance-toolkit
tools.how: Its Agent SRE layer ships a kill switch, SLO/error-budget monitoring and circuit breakers that halt a runaway failing agent loop; aimed at generic error-rate runaways, not fix-spirals specifically.

star_modes.name: Context pollution
star_modes.description: The agent's working context degrades over a session — relevant prior information is dropped, irrelevant material accumulates, or hallucinations from earlier turns are treated as ground truth in later turns.
star_modes.note: No dedicated detector for coding agents yet. The three that detect it are LLM-judge knowledge-retention scores built for chat assistants; several others only work on agents built with them.

tools.name: AutoGen
tools.how: Built-in OpenTelemetry tracing lets a human inspect drift; its buffered/head-tail contexts are token budgeting, not an anti-degradation mechanism.

tools.name: agno
tools.how: Traces runs and tool calls so a human can diagnose drift; no built-in context-pollution check.

tools.name: LangGraph
tools.how: Memory docs name stale or off-topic context as a failure and ship trim/remove/summarize message utilities that the developer must apply; no detection.

tools.name: mlflow
tools.how: Built-in multi-turn KnowledgeRetention LLM judge (experimental) checks whether the assistant retains information from earlier user inputs.

tools.name: mastra
tools.how: Observational Memory compresses old messages into observations so the agent reads what matters instead of stale tool output over long sessions.

tools.name: opik
tools.how: Conversation-thread metrics (Knowledge Retention, Degeneration) check that later replies keep earlier user facts and flag repetition/degeneration.

tools.name: DeepEval
tools.how: Multi-turn LLM-judge metrics (Knowledge Retention, Turn Relevancy) score whether a conversation keeps earlier facts and stays on task.

tools.name: Arize Phoenix
